source.title: ColorBench: Can VLMs See and Understand the Colorful World? A Comprehensive Benchmark for Color Perception, Reasoning, and Robustness
source.authors: Yijun Liang; Ming Li; Chenrui Fan; Ziyue Li; Dang Nguyen; Kwesi Cobbina; Shweta Bhardwaj; Jiuhai Chen; Fuxiao Liu; Tianyi Zhou

record.tranche_reason: Extends the question of scale-related downstream performance to vision-language models evaluated on a color benchmark, using rank correlations rather than held-out language-model loss.
record.gate_note: The study reports correlations between VLM size and benchmark accuracy, which bear on V6. Its language-model pretraining-loss, token-count, compute-optimal-allocation, and fixed-parameter architecture results are not tested. CoT, grayscale, fine-tuning, and individual benchmark results are not rows here because they do not test a scaling version; the table of model accuracies is also not separately extracted because the study reports the relevant size-performance correlations in Table 2.
record.test_reason: The study reports Spearman correlations between ColorBench accuracy and model size across existing VLMs (0.5B–78B). This bears on V6 (downstream performance improves with scale) in a new setting: vision-language models on color tasks. The evidence is weak in kind. The models are uncontrolled, span many families with different training recipes, have no matched compute or data, and no predictive fit is made. It bears on no loss-based version.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors say the 'scaling law (larger models are better)' still holds on ColorBench but is much weaker, and depends mainly on language-model size. They say vision-encoder correlations are not significant because few vision-encoder sizes exist in current VLMs, not because there is no effect. They also note that performance gaps between small and large models, and between open and proprietary models, are small. The record's phrase 'weaker than they characterize for scaling generally' should read simply 'much weaker'.
record.recipe_differences: Uses benchmark accuracy and Spearman rank correlations across existing VLMs rather than controlled language-model training runs and held-out cross-entropy loss; no power-law fit or compute-optimal allocation is estimated.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported correlations vary by task and by whether size means L+V, language-model size, or vision-encoder size.
record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2025 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks
record.problems: The evidence is rank correlation across a set of existing VLMs, not controlled scaling experiments or predictive fits. The authors note that vision-encoder choices and sizes are limited in current models, constraining conclusions about vision-encoder scaling. Exact p-values are not reported; the table only marks correlations with p-values ≤ 0.05.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 reports task accuracies for individual VLMs, but those individual entries are not separately extracted because Table 2 reports the study's aggregated size-performance correlations used for V6. Other non-scaling findings, including CoT, grayscale, and fine-tuning results, are outside the tested claim versions.

untested.parts: All of it. No pretraining loss, token or compute scaling, and no power-law fit.
All of it. No fitted law is extrapolated.
All of it. No compute-optimal allocation.
All of it. No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss in VLMs. Only rank correlations of accuracy are given, with no loss and no power-law form.
Prediction from pretraining loss; an explicit predictive functional fit; controlled scaling with recipe held fixed; any extrapolation to larger models.
All of it. No fitting choices are compared.

missing.what: Within-family size ordering: larger models score higher within each family on P&R Overall and robustness. This is the most controlled size comparison in the paper.
missing.locator: Figure 4; Appendix L.1 Figures 26–35; L.3 Figures 41–47

missing.what: Average RGB+Text P&R Overall accuracy by LLM size group rises monotonically: 37.4, 41.1, 43.2, 46.2, 47.6.
Best model per size group: P&R Overall rises from 41.5 (<7B) to 51.9 (>70B); robustness rises from 63.7 to 86.2. The authors stress that the gaps are small.

record.verdict_notes: 'Scaling law' here means only a positive rank correlation between benchmark accuracy and parameter count across heterogeneous off-the-shelf VLMs. There is no power law, no loss and no control of data or compute, so the evidence on V6 is weak. It is unclear how many models entered the correlations: proprietary models of unknown size were presumably excluded, so N is likely below 32. Exact p-values are not given. Whether VLMs count as the 'same kind of system' for a language-model scaling claim is debatable; I treated V6 as bearing on any model scale versus downstream task.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute; bottleneck conditions; several orders of magnitude.
Extrapolation of loss fits from smaller to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and how either allocation grows with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests accuracy correlations with model-part sizes on ColorBench, but not prediction from pretraining loss, an explicit predictive fit, or downstream tasks beyond this benchmark.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and systematic bending of loss curves.

relationships.condition: P&R Overall and robustness, and most perception/reasoning tasks, against total (L+V) or language-model size
relationships.reason: Positive significant Spearman correlations, 0.51–0.76 for total size and 0.47–0.76 for language size, on overall, robustness and most tasks (R01–R05, R07, R11–R13, R15, R17, R19, R23–R24). Correlation only, with no predictive fit.
relationships.display_finding: Overall, robustness and most task scores have significant positive Spearman correlations of 0.51–0.76 with total size and 0.47–0.76 with language-model size.

relationships.condition: C'Count, C'Mimic, C'Extract and C'Prop against total or language size
relationships.reason: Significant but weaker positive correlations, 0.43–0.49 (R06, R09, R14, R16, R18, R21). The authors call the scaling 'much weaker' for color tasks.
relationships.display_finding: Correlations with total or language-model size were significantly positive but modest at 0.43–0.49.

relationships.condition: Vision-encoder size: overall, robustness and several tasks
relationships.reason: Significant positive correlations of 0.53–0.62 for O'Recog, C'Prop, C'Comp, C'Mimic, P&R Overall and C'Robust (R27–R29, R33, R35–R36).
relationships.display_finding: Vision-encoder size has significant positive correlations of 0.53–0.62 with O'Recog, C'Prop, C'Comp, C'Mimic, P&R Overall and C'Robust scores.

relationships.condition: Vision-encoder size on C'Recog, C'Extract, C'Count, O'Count and C'Illu
relationships.reason: Correlations are weak or non-significant (R25, R26, R30, R31, R32). The authors attribute this to most VLMs using 300–400M encoders, so scale was barely varied.
relationships.display_finding: Correlations with vision-encoder size were weak or nonsignificant, attributed to most encoders occupying the narrow 300–400M range.

relationships.condition: Color Illusion task, total and language size
relationships.reason: Language-size correlation is significantly negative (-0.3697, R20); total-size correlation is negative but not significant (R08).
relationships.display_finding: Performance correlated significantly negatively with language size at −0.3697, while its negative correlation with total size was nonsignificant.

relationships.condition: Color Blindness task, all size measures
relationships.reason: No significant correlation with total (0.246), language (0.282) or vision (-0.068) size (R10, R22, R34). The authors name it as an exception to scaling.
relationships.display_finding: Correlations with total, language and vision size were nonsignificant at 0.246, 0.282 and −0.068, respectively.
